text: Hemorrhagic Septicemia (HS) is caused by the bacterium Pasteurella Multocida Type B; buffaloes are more susceptible than cattle. Incubation is very short — an animal can sicken within hours of contact with a sick animal. Death occurs 6–24 hours after onset, but typical signs are visible before death: reluctance to move, high fever, salivation and watery nasal discharge, respiratory distress with bloody discharge, and swelling of the head, neck, and brisket. Necropsy shows a light-yellow, gelatinous swelling in the jaw and neck. Treatment: the disease progresses too fast to treat reliably, but IV Sulfonamide, IV Tetracycline, or Enrofloxacin are recommended, with the first injection at double dose (20 mg/kg); treating in-contact cattle too can stop the disease in incubation. Prevention: vaccinate every 6 months, ideally timed before the rainy season; calves get good protection from maternal antibodies if the dam is vaccinated during the last months of pregnancy.
